planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring once soil has warmed; Cape Breeze was discovered as a naturally occurring selection in a sandy coastal garden and tolerates salt spray and dune conditions exceptionally well.

directions: A compact, dense switchgrass with narrow blue-green blades that arch outward from a tidy crown shorter than most switchgrass cultivars. Light pink flower plumes open in late summer and age to a lightly toasted tan, appearing earlier in the season and holding green foliage later into fall than typical Panicum virgatum. Its salt and wind tolerance make it an excellent choice for coastal gardens, dunes, and roadside plantings. Cut back old growth in late winter before new shoots emerge.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun; forms an upright, compact clump reaching full size in its second growing season.

directions: Wide, bluish leaves build an upright, compact clump topped in late summer by a dense cloud of soft pink seedheads held just above the foliage. Fall brings a pinkish-gold color shift that extends seasonal interest well into autumn. This switchgrass adapts to both dry and moist soils and needs no fertilizer or staking once established. Shear the dried clump to a few inches in late winter before new growth begins.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring, spacing 24-30 inches apart in full sun; part of the Prairie Winds switchgrass series bred for sturdy, non-flopping stems.

directions: Blue-green leaves form an elegant, strongly upright clump that resists the late-season flopping common in older switchgrass cultivars. Brilliant rosy-purple seedheads appear in late summer and persist as a fall highlight that gives the cultivar its name. Mid-sized among switchgrass selections, it works well as a specimen, in sweeping drifts, or softening pond and stream edges. Cut the dried foliage to the ground in late winter before spring growth resumes.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in full sun; this tall, upright selection needs little support thanks to strong drought, heat, and wind tolerance.

directions: Wide, strappy blue-green leaves build a tall, sturdy clump that remains upright through summer storms without staking. Greenish-tan flower panicles burst from the upper two-thirds of the plant from midsummer into fall, resembling spray from a fountain, and the foliage turns clear yellow before winter dormancy. Excellent as a dramatic specimen or for screening at the back of a border. Cut the old clump down in late winter before new shoots emerge.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring, giving room for a dense, upright clump; tolerates everything from moist to very dry soils once established.

directions: Steel-blue, gunmetal-grey leaves pack densely into a robust, compact, upright clump. Starting in late summer, airy plumes of smoky purple rise above the foliage and fade to tan, persisting as winter interest into the colder months. Low-maintenance once established, it attracts butterflies and birds and hosts several skipper caterpillars. The only required care is cutting the dried clump back in late winter before new growth starts.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring; one of the most compact switchgrass selections, suited to the front or middle of a border where full-size cultivars would be too large.

directions: A dwarf, densely upright switchgrass that stays far smaller than the species, making it useful as a small-scale hedge or border accent. Dark rosy-red seedheads cover the top of the plant in fall as the foliage turns brilliant yellow, and the sturdy stems shrug off heavy winter snow without flattening. Deer generally leave it alone, and it needs only low to consistent moisture once established. Cut the clump back in late winter before spring growth begins.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in any soil from sand to clay; tolerates periodic flooding as well as drought once established, and takes salt spray well in coastal or roadside plantings.

directions: Blue-green spring foliage deepens through summer into an intensely saturated wine-red by late summer, more vivid than older red-leaved switchgrass cultivars like 'Shenandoah'. Late-season flower plumes echo the foliage in reddish tones, rising above the compact, upright, clump-forming habit. It withstands wind and salt, making it a reliable choice for seaside gardens and roadside plantings as well as mixed borders. Cut the dried clump to the ground in late winter before new shoots appear.
